{{DISPLAYTITLE:Dependent function types}}
{{Plebeian|Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Propositions as types|Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Types as specifications}}
{{Lean theorem prover map}}

A '''dependent function type''' is the type of functions whose result type may vary with the
argument. In Lean it is written <code>(x : A) → B</code>, where <code>B</code> may mention
<code>x</code>, and in the literature it is often written
<math>\Pi x : A.\, B</math>. It is the only kind of function type in Lean's core theory. The
ordinary arrow <code>A → B</code>, universal quantification <code>∀ x : A, P x</code> and
implication <code>P → Q</code> are all instances of it. This page gives its rules, shows how
the familiar forms arise as special cases, and explains the implicit and instance-implicit
arguments that the elaborator adds on top of the same type.

== What the type means ==

Given a type <code>A</code> and, for each <code>a : A</code>, a type <code>B a</code>, a
function <code>f : (x : A) → B x</code> is a function that sends each <code>a : A</code> to
an element <code>f a</code> of <code>B a</code>. The type of the result depends on the
argument.<ref name="tpil">Jeremy Avigad, Leonardo de Moura, Soonho Kong and Sebastian
Ullrich, ''Theorem Proving in Lean 4'', lean-lang.org (version for Lean 4.33.0), chapter 2,
"Dependent Type Theory".
https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/Dependent-Type-Theory/</ref> Read as sets,
such a function is an element of the product <math>\prod_{a \in A} B(a)</math>, which is why
these types are also called '''dependent products''' or <math>\Pi</math>-types.<ref name="refman-fn">''The
Lean Language Reference'', for Lean 4.34.0, lean-lang.org, 2026, section 4.1, "Functions".
https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/The-Type-System/Functions/</ref>

A small example: <code>Fin k</code> is the type of natural numbers less than
<code>k</code>, so a function that returns the number 0 as an element of
<code>Fin (n + 1)</code> has a different result type for every <code>n</code>.

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
def zeroFin : (n : Nat) → Fin (n + 1) := fun n => ⟨0, Nat.succ_pos n⟩

#check zeroFin 4
#check zeroFin 0
</pre>

Lean 4.34.1 prints <code>zeroFin 4 : Fin (4 + 1)</code> and
<code>zeroFin 0 : Fin (0 + 1)</code>: one function, two result types.

== The rules ==

The type has the usual four kinds of rule, in the notation of
[[Lean theorem prover/Foundations/Terms, types and judgments|Terms, types and judgments]].
They are Carneiro's rules for Lean, with <math>\mathrm{Sort}\,u</math> for his
<math>\mathrm{U}_u</math>; as on that page, the introduction rule also requires the domain
to be a type.<ref name="carneiro2019">Mario Carneiro, ''The Type Theory of
Lean'', MSc thesis, Carnegie Mellon University, 2019.
https://github.com/digama0/lean-type-theory/releases/tag/v1.0</ref>

'''Formation.''' A dependent function type exists when its domain is a type and its codomain
is a type in the context extended by the bound variable:

:<math>\frac{\Gamma \vdash A : \mathrm{Sort}\,u \qquad \Gamma, x : A \vdash B : \mathrm{Sort}\,v}{\Gamma \vdash (x : A) \to B : \mathrm{Sort}\,(\mathrm{imax}\,u\,v)}</math>

The universe of the result is <math>\mathrm{imax}\,u\,v</math>, which equals
<math>\max(u, v)</math> unless <math>v = 0</math>, in which case it is 0. That exception
makes a function type whose codomain is a proposition itself a proposition, whatever its
domain; why it is
needed is the subject of [[Lean theorem prover/Foundations/Universes and Prop|Universes and Prop]].

'''Introduction.''' A function is made by abstraction. If <math>A</math> is a type and
<math>e</math> has type <math>B</math> when <math>x : A</math> is assumed, then
<math>\lambda x : A.\, e</math> has the dependent function type:

:<math>\frac{\Gamma \vdash A : \mathrm{Sort}\,u \qquad \Gamma, x : A \vdash e : B}{\Gamma \vdash \lambda x : A.\, e : (x : A) \to B}</math>

'''Elimination.''' A function is used by application, and the argument is substituted into
the result type:

:<math>\frac{\Gamma \vdash f : (x : A) \to B \qquad \Gamma \vdash a : A}{\Gamma \vdash f\,a : B[a/x]}</math>

The substitution <math>B[a/x]</math> is where dependency shows: in the example above,
<math>B</math> is <code>Fin (n + 1)</code> and applying to 4 gives
<code>Fin (4 + 1)</code>.

'''Computation and uniqueness.''' Applying an abstraction reduces by substitution, the
'''beta''' rule; and every function equals the abstraction of its own application, the
'''eta''' rule:

:<math>(\lambda x : A.\, e)\,a \equiv e[a/x] \qquad\qquad \lambda x : A.\, f\,x \equiv f</math>

Both are definitional equalities in Lean, so both can be proved by <code>rfl</code>:

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
example : (fun x : Nat => x + 1) 2 = 3 := rfl
example (f : Nat → Nat) : (fun x => f x) = f := rfl
</pre>

Definitional equality of functions goes no further than this. Two functions that agree on
every argument but are computed differently are not, in general, definitionally equal; that
they are equal is a theorem, <code>funext</code>, which Lean proves using quotient
types.<ref name="refman-fn" /> See [[Lean theorem prover/Foundations/Definitional equality|Definitional equality]] and [[Lean theorem prover/Foundations/Quotient types|Quotient types]].

In the core language every function takes exactly one argument. A function "of two
arguments" is a function that returns a function, and Lean's notation for several arguments
is an abbreviation for this nesting.<ref name="refman-fn" />

== The arrow is the non-dependent case ==

When <code>B</code> does not mention <code>x</code>, the type <code>(x : A) → B</code> is
written <code>A → B</code>. Nothing else changes: the core language has only one function
type, and a non-dependent function type is a dependent one whose bound variable is
unused.<ref name="refman-fn" /> Lean confirms that the two spellings denote the same type:

<pre class="lean lean-cont" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
example : ((x : Nat) → Bool) = (Nat → Bool) := rfl
</pre>

The same construction gives the logical connectives. When <code>B</code> is a proposition,
<code>(x : A) → B</code> is the proposition "for every <code>x : A</code>, <code>B</code>",
and Lean prints it with <code>∀</code>. When moreover <code>A</code> is a proposition and
<code>B</code> does not mention <code>x</code>, it is the implication <code>A → B</code>. A
proof of a universal statement is a function from instances to proofs, and using the
statement is applying the function:

<pre class="lean lean-cont" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
theorem add_zero' : ∀ n : Nat, n + 0 = n := fun n => Nat.add_zero n

#check add_zero' 5
#check fun (p q : Prop) (hp : p) (_ : q) => hp
</pre>

The output is <code>add_zero' 5 : 5 + 0 = 5</code> and
<code>fun p q hp x => hp : ∀ (p q : Prop), p → q → p</code>. The second term is a proof of
the propositional tautology <math>p \to (q \to p)</math>, and its type is printed with
<code>∀</code> for the dependent binders and <code>→</code> for the others. This
correspondence between propositions and types, proofs and terms, is described in plain
language in [[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Propositions as types|Propositions as types]].

== Implicit and instance-implicit arguments ==

A binder in a function type carries a mark saying how the elaborator should supply the
argument at a call site:<ref name="refman-fntypes">''The Lean Language Reference'', for Lean
4.34.0, lean-lang.org, 2026, section 13.2, "Function Types".
https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Terms/Function-Types/</ref>

* <code>(x : A)</code>, '''explicit''': the caller writes the argument.
* <code>{x : A}</code>, '''implicit''': the elaborator inserts a placeholder and fills it by unification, from the other arguments and the expected type.
* <code>⦃x : A⦄</code>, '''strict implicit''': as implicit, but the placeholder is inserted only once a later explicit argument is given.
* <code>[C]</code> or <code>[inst : C]</code>, '''instance implicit''': the elaborator finds the argument by type class instance synthesis ([[Lean theorem prover/System/Type classes and instance resolution|Type classes and instance resolution]]).

The mark is stored in the term as a <code>BinderInfo</code> field of the binder. It is
information for the elaborator only. It does not affect type checking or definitional
equality in the core theory, and two function types that differ only in it are
definitionally equal.<ref name="refman-fn" />

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
import Lean
open Lean Meta

def double {α : Type} [inst : Add α] (x : α) : α := x + x

#check @double
#eval double 21
#eval @double Nat instAddNat 21
example : ({α : Type} → α → α) = ((α : Type) → α → α) := rfl

#eval show MetaM Unit from do
  let some c := (← getEnv).find? ``double | throwError "missing"
  IO.println (repr c.type)
</pre>

<code>#check @double</code> prints <code>@double : {α : Type} → [inst : Add α] → α → α</code>;
the <code>@</code> asks for every argument to be shown and accepted explicitly. Both
evaluations print <code>42</code>: in the first the elaborator found <code>α := Nat</code> by
unification and the instance <code>instAddNat</code> by synthesis; in the second both were
written out. The <code>example</code> is accepted, so an implicit and an explicit binder give
definitionally equal types. The last command prints the stored type of
<code>double</code>:

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
Lean.Expr.forallE
  `α
  (Lean.Expr.sort (Lean.Level.succ (Lean.Level.zero)))
  (Lean.Expr.forallE
    `inst
    (Lean.Expr.app (Lean.Expr.const `Add [Lean.Level.zero]) (Lean.Expr.bvar 0))
    (Lean.Expr.forallE `x (Lean.Expr.bvar 1) (Lean.Expr.bvar 2) (Lean.BinderInfo.default))
    (Lean.BinderInfo.instImplicit))
  (Lean.BinderInfo.implicit)
</pre>

It is three nested <code>forallE</code> binders, as for any function of three arguments; the
only trace of the braces and brackets is the last field of each binder,
<code>implicit</code>, <code>instImplicit</code> and <code>default</code>. To the core theory,
<code>double</code> is a function of three explicit arguments, the first a type and the
second a structure of operations on it.

Implicit arguments are a convenience, and they can fail. When nothing determines an implicit
argument, the elaborator reports it rather than guessing:

<pre class="lean lean-fails" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
def nothing := List.nil
</pre>

Lean 4.34.1 reports <code>don't know how to synthesize implicit argument `α`</code>, showing
the partial term <code>@List.nil ?m.3</code>, in which <code>?m.3</code> is the unfilled
placeholder: no element type for the empty list was given or can be inferred.

== Polymorphism ==

Because a domain may itself be a universe, the same type expresses polymorphism. The
identity function is a single term of type <code>{α : Sort u} → α → α</code>:

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
#check @id
</pre>

Lean prints <code>@id : {α : Sort u_1} → α → α</code>. Its first argument is a type, and the type of its
second argument depends on the first. There is no separate mechanism for generic functions:
a generic function is a dependent function whose first argument is a type. Quantifying over
types this way raises the question of what universe the function type itself lives in, which
is answered by the <math>\mathrm{imax}</math> in the formation rule and taken up on the next
page.
